<!-- Dictation part 1 (2026-11-25). Comments marked CHECK are open questions; they do not appear in the PDF. -->

This first essay is on John Mearsheimer's video lecture "Why China Cannot Rise Peacefully," the title it has on YouTube (Centre for International Policy Studies uOttawa, 2012). I think John Mearsheimer is a realist in his perspective (Bak, 2026). At the beginning of his lecture, he states five key assumptions. First, no authority sits above states; there is anarchy among states. Second, all states have some offensive military capability. Third, no state can be certain about the intentions of another state. Fourth, the principal goal of every state (not the only goal, but the principal goal) is survival. Fifth, each state is a rational actor. He later says that he views each state as a black box (Bak, 2026), somewhat like an individual: domestic politics aside, it is a rational actor regardless of what is going on behind the scenes.

The result of these assumptions is that states fear each other. There is no 911 to call, and the reason they fear each other is that there is no one to call for backup when they get into trouble. He also states that, given the anarchy among states, the best survival mechanism for a state is to be powerful, and specifically, the best position is to be a regional hegemon (Bak, 2026). In his mind, a global hegemon is not very possible. The U.S., he says, is trying to be one but is relatively unsuccessful. The reason the U.S. has such a large global presence is that it is such a great regional hegemon in the Western Hemisphere that it is "free to roam." Because it is free to roam, it can project power in other places in the world, such as Europe or Asia. Other countries cannot do that because they do not have the regional hegemony the U.S. does.

That is also the reason he believes China cannot rise peacefully. At the end of the day, U.S. foreign policy is about preventing other states from having an impact on the U.S. The U.S. uses its ability to roam to prevent other states from becoming regional hegemons that would also be able to roam and project power across the globe. He cites U.S. foreign policy since the 1700s: the U.S. dominating the continental U.S., then the Monroe Doctrine and the Spanish-American War, where the U.S. really starts to establish its regional hegemony, and then U.S. foreign policy since World War I and World War II. Since the world wars, the main focus of U.S. power projection has been Europe. With the fall of the Soviet Union, though, that power projection has changed, and the U.S. is starting to shift more of its effort towards Asia.

This is especially true nowadays. His lecture is from 14 years ago, so his prediction holds up pretty well, because U.S. foreign policy has shifted away from Europe. Donald Trump consistently states that Europe needs to pull its fair share and that the U.S. will not always be around. You can see resources shifting towards what Mearsheimer deems the three strategic areas of the world that matter to the U.S.: Europe, the Persian Gulf, and Northeast Asia.

One of the reasons he cites for China not being able to establish regional hegemony is not just U.S. power projection but also China's neighbors in the region, like Japan, India, and Russia, which would theoretically fear its rise. If China rises to the power of a regional hegemon, that suppresses their ability to have a say in their own region, and they do not like that. But none of them is as powerful as China or able to resist it without the U.S. As a result, in his mind, many of those countries would not want the U.S. to leave Asia.

But this idea does not hold up super well, because BRICS has grown since his lecture, and it is an allyship between Russia, India, and China, as well as Brazil. In that sense, some of China's neighbors (I would argue, those that feel they have some equivalence of power) are willing to partner with China as a means to grow past the U.S. and outside of U.S. influence. That seems to be the trend since his lecture: some powers are willing to go against the U.S. and side with China. Still, countries like Japan and the Philippines are very much interested in keeping the U.S. presence in Asia.

The U.S. is also very interested in keeping its presence in Asia because of semiconductor manufacturing in Taiwan. That is controversial because, according to China, there is no Taiwan; there is only the island of Taiwan, which belongs to China. It is a dilemma for both powers, neither of which has made a move yet, but it is a signal to the world. If China were ever to make a move on Taiwan, it would be broadcasting not just to the region but to the world that it believes it is more capable as a regional hegemon than the U.S. is at projecting power and protecting its allies: "We believe we can take Taiwan and make it truly ours."

That has many strategic implications because of the global reliance on semiconductors. Not just our manufacturing but also our information economies, which are more common in the Western Hemisphere, depend on cheap and efficient semiconductor manufacturing. If China takes TSMC, it will likely gain a massive advantage over the U.S. in semiconductor manufacturing. China is currently trying, in its own way, to win that race through domestic production, but there is a lot of ground to cover, so at the end of the day it would be more beneficial just to have TSMC under its control. The U.S. is mitigating this by trying to move semiconductor manufacturing onto U.S. shores. It has an advantage because it is directly partnered with TSMC, so some knowledge sharing smooths that process (National Institute of Standards and Technology [NIST], n.d.; TSMC, 2025). Still, semiconductor manufacturing is an incredibly complex industry, and it takes decades to achieve the kind of production TSMC currently has. So it is a race in that sense, which is why you see things like the CHIPS Act: the U.S. is effectively trying to prevent China from doing what it has done with much of its industry, which is to steal U.S. intellectual property and then reproduce it at a cheaper scale, resulting in a hollowing out of U.S. industry. The U.S. is trying to prevent that from happening with chips, but chips are a really unique industry. That is where the main fight between the U.S. and China is right now.

There is also military positioning. China currently tries to flex its position by claiming historic rights to nearly all the waters inside its nine-dash line, a claim the U.S. State Department says does not accord with international law and an international tribunal rejected in 2016 (Gupta & Geraci, 2020; U.S. Department of State, 2014). This has been China's official position since its 1992 Law on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone, which claims the South China Sea on the basis of historical rights and a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea around the island groups China claims (Council on Foreign Relations, 2024; U.S. Department of State, 2014). In practice, by claiming the sea's features as territory and drawing a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea around each of them, China gives itself a basis to contest passage across much of the South China Sea. China also builds up existing islands and creates new ones there (Council on Foreign Relations, 2026). China tries to say that the South China Sea is all Chinese; that is how it projects power there.

<!-- Dictation part 2 (2026-11-25). -->

Another point Mearsheimer makes is the U.S. protection of the Monroe Doctrine in the 21st century. A big reason the U.S. wants to have such an impact in Asia is that its main goal is to protect its regional hegemony, which also means projecting its power across other regions of the globe. It is able to do this because of the Monroe Doctrine, established back in 1823. This occurred after his lecture, but recently Chinese relations with Venezuela became quite strong, and as a result, Donald Trump, who previously had not had a large concern with Venezuela, became very concerned with it. If you look at the news media, much of the stated reasoning was about narco-terrorism and similar issues. The reality, however, is that Venezuela was providing China with a lot of oil (U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission [USCC], 2026), and Venezuela had also become the largest buyer of Chinese military equipment in Latin America (USCC, 2026). The U.S. had a vested interest in intervening in Venezuela, not only to limit Chinese oil imports but also to prevent the normalization of Chinese influence in Latin America. The U.S. viewed this as a violation of the Monroe Doctrine, and to prevent those Chinese relations from growing, it removed Maduro from power and installed a friendly regime, really just Maduro's vice president, Delcy Rodríguez (Phillips, 2026). Venezuela's oil sales to China collapsed almost immediately. Trump has said China is still free to buy Venezuelan oil at fair market prices, but that has largely stopped, and the largest share of Venezuela's oil exports now goes to the U.S. (Parraga, 2026). So you can see that the U.S. still has a very large interest in protecting the Monroe Doctrine, very comparable to the Cuban Missile Crisis back in the 1960s. The U.S. pursuit of its own regional hegemony shows that U.S. interest in Asia is really about preventing China from establishing its own regional hegemony.

One of the assumptions he makes early on is that China will continue to grow, and I want to challenge that assumption. Fourteen years ago, China was by far the fastest-growing economy in the world, and it still continues to have relatively strong growth. But several issues have popped up that will probably prevent it from sustaining that growth. This is more opinion-based, but the reality is that China's housing industry is crashing, it is going to experience imminent population collapse (Bouey et al., 2026), and the U.S. and many information economies around the world are making a concerted effort to prevent China from continuing to steal IP. So the techniques China used to grow its industry probably will not continue to be as successful. I am not saying they will stop, but they will not be as successful, which means innovation and growth will have to come through more natural means.

The big challenge here is that RAND projects China could lose about 250 million of its 1.4 billion people by 2050, which is quite stark. By then, people 65 and older could make up nearly a third of the population, with fewer than two working-age adults for every person 65 and older, and China's younger age groups are much smaller than its older ones (Bouey et al., 2026). The U.S. currently experiences a less pronounced version of this, and so does Europe. This means the entire care industry for these older populations depends on far fewer younger workers. Younger workers in China are also less willing to work for lower wages, because they are not used to farm life or the days when China was an agrarian society. China is now a very industrialized society, and its younger people are not willing to work longer hours for cheaper pay. They are more interested in being involved with capital and that side of the economy, which does not have as much labor demand. So China's industry is itself struggling. Does that mean China is going to stop growing? By no means. It will continue to grow and continue to be strong, but it probably will not outright surpass the U.S. at the pace we expected 14 years ago. Instead, it will probably see a slowdown over the next one to two decades, simply because it does not have the bodies to support the continued growth of its industries, and its economy is currently being kept afloat by massive government stimulus. That can work for a long time, but it can only work for so long. So China has several issues that make continued growth at this rate quite dubious.

The other challenge China is going to face is military competition. The Russia–Ukraine war has shown that a smaller nation can resist a much larger and better-equipped nation quite effectively in the modern day. Ukraine is a smaller nation with a massive land border, which is much harder to defend than a coastline, yet it has held a much larger Russian force to very costly and very small gains, and is still doing so. Now imagine what a war over Taiwan would cost China. It would cost quite a bit.

A Chinese invasion of Taiwan would require far more complex military operations, against a force better equipped and more capable than Ukraine's was at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. China would have to cross the Taiwan Strait with a massive force, and seas calm enough for a crossing in force come only in narrow windows, roughly April to May and September to October (Sorensen, 2026). Amphibious operations depend heavily on weather, especially sea states; even the PLA's own amphibious training is concentrated between roughly March and September (Blasko, 2024, pp. 71–72). Sealift would also be the primary link carrying the largest volume of forces and supplies across the strait (McCauley, 2024, p. 308), so the weather would have to hold not only for the landing but for the supply lines that follow it. Unlike the U.S. in 1944, China could not route its supply around the strait; it would have to push everything across it, through both the weather and U.S. naval and strike assets. The United States planned exactly this kind of operation during World War II, when Taiwan was under Japanese control. That plan, Operation Causeway, would have been the largest amphibious campaign in the Pacific Theater and the largest sea-air-land engagement in world history (Easton, 2024). U.S. planners estimated it would need a force of 776,913, including all six divisions of the Marine Corps (Easton, 2024, p. 20). A U.S. force that was highly experienced at amphibious invasions, with far more amphibious capacity than China has today, ultimately decided that the force needed to take and hold Taiwan was so large that the operation was effectively moot; Japan had made the island too difficult to attack at a cost the Americans could justify (Easton, 2024, p. 28). That decision also came at a time when Japan's military capability was greatly waning. By contrast, the PLA today lacks the amphibious lift to carry even the roughly 30,000 personnel of its six amphibious combined-arms brigades (Blasko, 2024, p. 75), and a major invasion would have to rely heavily on civilian ships (Erickson et al., 2024, p. 11). Imagine the same operation conducted against a much more modern and better-supplied force, on a much more prepared island, with much stronger support from U.S. precision strike assets. It is more likely impossible, let alone costly.

The scale of that plan is striking. Planners sketched an operation that would rival the D-Day landings in Normandy (Easton, 2024, p. 9), where nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed on the first day (National WWII Museum, n.d.). Yet when those estimates were drawn up in mid-1944, U.S. intelligence put the Japanese garrison on Taiwan at only about 35,000 troops (Easton, 2024, p. 22). Taiwan's military today has 169,000 active personnel and about 1.66 million reservists (DefenseMatrixLab, 2026), nearly five times that 1944 estimate in active troops alone. If the U.S. judged that a force of roughly 777,000 was needed against a garrison of about 35,000, consider the force and resources it would take to overcome a far better prepared defender several times larger, without the naval dominance the U.S. held when it considered Operation Causeway. And along with the demographic collapse, the Chinese military will likely not be able to grow as large as it could be. It is probably at the peak of its military potential: if China started a draft and mobilization today, it would be more successful in fielding a larger, more capable army than it would be 10 years from now. So China has a real dilemma on its hands, because as it stands, it probably would not be able to take Taiwan. It would be incredibly costly and would almost certainly affect China's ability to continue to be a regional hegemon. If China won, the victory would almost certainly be Pyrrhic. That gives China an incentive not to take Taiwan. At the same time, if it does not take Taiwan and allows U.S. interests to continue in the region unhindered, it cannot project the power needed to become the dominant regional hegemon that Mearsheimer predicts it can be.

So there are definitely some issues for China. It does have allies, at least in the sense that Russia, North Korea, and India are supportive, but only insofar as it helps their own ends. Russia, India, and Brazil are allies economically, not necessarily militarily. In any conflict in which the U.S. and its regional allies decide to fight China, you probably are not going to see Russia jump into that war. You might see North Korea join, but you probably would not see countries like India or Russia jump in, despite their significant economic partnerships with China. Instead, they would probably stay out of it, so China would be largely on its own in any fight. Granted, China still has a massive population and a massive production and manufacturing industry, so there is no doubt it would be quite capable militarily. But combine U.S. regional allies with the U.S.'s main focus, and think back to World War II. As Mearsheimer points out, and as I agree, the U.S. defeated a very powerful Japan virtually on its own (Centre for International Policy Studies uOttawa, 2012, 26:25), and much of that was because it was able to outproduce Japan and because the island of Japan was very isolated. Japan had to sustain a large navy to protect its ability to project power, and it could not do that over time. The U.S. simply outproduced Japan and had more resources. The same may not be said today, but China is a significant importer of oil (Downs, 2026; U.S. Energy Information Administration [EIA], 2026; Worldometer, n.d.), and oil would always be the first problem, because a massive military requires a massive stock of oil to run. China's own production covers only 32.6% of what it consumes (Worldometer, n.d.). The U.S., on its own, is able to produce enough oil to field its entire military, as well as those of several of its major allies in the region. So the U.S. has a major advantage in oil, and China does not.

<!-- Added 2026-11-25 (typed, not dictated). -->

Another interesting point is the historical reality of Japanese reliance on U.S. oil before World War II. When the U.S. restricted oil exports to Japan, that was in fact a large part of Japan's decision to go to war with the U.S. This is another reason China has major incentives not to be reliant on U.S. oil. Trump, for his part, has put a large share of China's oil imports under U.S. control by restricting Venezuelan oil to China (Parraga, 2026) and through the current naval blockade of Iranian oil (Institute for the Study of War & Critical Threats Project, 2026). Together, Iran and Venezuela supplied about 15% of China's crude imports in 2025 (Downs, 2026). In effect, the U.S. can control enough of China's oil imports to keep it from sustaining large-scale combat operations over a long period. Without the ability, or the credible threat of the ability, to conduct large-scale combat operations, China cannot establish the regional hegemony that would let it "free-roam." This is yet another way the U.S. projects its power in the region.

<!-- Dictation part 3: policy recommendations (2026-11-25). -->

In terms of policy recommendations, I think the U.S. is in a very strong position for the future. China has a lot of reasons not to invade Taiwan. The U.S. does not even really need to sign any agreement stating that it will defend Taiwan. It just needs to continue giving China the perception that if anything were to happen to Taiwan, the U.S. would defend it, and I think the U.S. currently does that very well. Shifting its global focus in power projection towards Asia makes a lot of sense. Asia and the Middle East continue to be regions of the world with significant strategic impact on the U.S.'s ability to remain a regional hegemon, so keeping its focus there makes a lot of sense. The U.S. already has a well-established position there, so it does not need to do anything other than maintain its power projection and continue to innovate technologically to stay ahead in the arms race.

So at the end of the day, my policy recommendation is really just to keep doing what the U.S. is doing. Do not allow China or any other power to establish strong connections in the Western Hemisphere. At the same time, the U.S. does not have to control Asia, but it does need to have the members of the region on its side and preserve its ability to project power. Effectively, the U.S. just needs to keep China in check, because China will not continue to grow as strong as it is forever. That would be very difficult, because China would need a miraculous shift in demographics. At the same time, China is in effect peaking in power, so the U.S. only really needs to prevent it from taking action while it is at the peak of its power. And the only thing the U.S. needs to do to prevent China from taking action is to give it the perception that the U.S. will take action. That is effectively what the current administration is attempting to do, especially with its actions in Venezuela, as well as its strict enforcement of export controls on advanced chips, which have had some controversy recently. Overall, the goal is to prevent China from being able to manufacture advanced semiconductors. Likewise, the U.S. is mitigating risk by moving semiconductor manufacturing into the U.S. and investing in its own country to be able to produce those things. This is what the CHIPS Act is for (NIST, n.d.), and it shows where the arms race, and quite frankly the manufacturing race, is happening. That is extremely wise, and the U.S. should continue to do it. It is actually a very bipartisan issue: the Biden administration passed the CHIPS Act, and the Trump administration has continued it (NIST, 2026). The U.S. policies that will most limit China's ability to become a regional hegemon are limiting its ability to steal intellectual property, diversifying semiconductor manufacturing, and keeping enough constraints in place that an invasion of Taiwan remains infeasible. From there, it becomes a waiting game for the U.S., as China's growth and its population advantage wane over the coming decades. So overall, my policy recommendation is effectively to keep doing what the U.S. is doing.
